lead: This unit teaches how a reinforced concrete beam is analysed and designed at the limit state of collapse in flexure, then checked for serviceability. You will size singly and doubly reinforced rectangular beams, T and L beams, use design aids, and compute deflection, crack control and cracking moment. After it you can take a beam's span, loads and materials and produce a safe reinforcement layout with the required checks.
about: Unit 2 covers limit state design of reinforced concrete beams in flexure and serviceability. Chapter 2.1 starts with singly reinforced rectangular beams. Chapter 2.2 classifies balanced, under-reinforced and over-reinforced sections. Chapter 2.3 adds compression steel for doubly reinforced beams. Chapter 2.4 extends the stress block to T and L flanged beams. Chapter 2.5 shows design aids for flexure, a short advanced topic. Chapter 2.6 checks deflection and crack control at service loads. Chapter 2.7 explains cracking moment and transformed sections, linking elastic behaviour to serviceability. The chapters move from one rectangular section to real floor beams and then to usability checks.

chapters.idea: A singly reinforced rectangular beam carries factored moment by a concrete compression block and a tension steel force, with the neutral axis found from strain compatibility.
chapters.depth: Cover IS 456 limit state flexure: plane sections remain plane; concrete tensile strength is ignored at collapse; the concrete stress block is 0.36 fck b xu with lever arm z = d − 0.42 xu; steel force is 0.87 fy Ast. Derive Mu = 0.36 fck b xu (d − 0.42 xu) = 0.87 fy Ast z; define b, d, D, xu, fck, fy and Ast. State xu,max/d = 0.53 for Fe250, 0.48 for Fe415, 0.46 for Fe500; check minimum steel 0.85 b d/fy and maximum 0.04 bD. Show the design sequence for a singly reinforced section. Some syllabi call this tension-only reinforcement.

figure.aria: Flowchart from beam data to limiting moment, then a check that chooses singly reinforced design or points to doubly reinforced design.

chapters.example: Design the tension steel for a singly reinforced rectangular beam: b = 230 mm, overall depth D = 450 mm, effective depth d = 400 mm, fck = 25 N/mm², fy = 415 N/mm², factored moment Mu = 120 kN·m. Check that the section is singly reinforced and give a bar arrangement.
chapters.trap: Using overall depth D in place of effective depth d, or using fy directly in place of 0.87 fy in the steel force, are the common errors.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: stress block parameters, characteristic strength and partial safety factors.
chapters.leave: Shear, torsion and bond go to Unit 3; slab design goes to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The amount of tension steel relative to the balanced steel sets the failure mode: steel yields first, concrete crushes first, or both happen together.
chapters.depth: Define balanced section when xu = xu,max, under-reinforced when xu < xu,max, over-reinforced when xu > xu,max. Use strain compatibility and concrete ultimate strain 0.0035 to show why steel yields first in under-reinforced sections. Give xu,max/d values and the balanced steel percentage pt,lim = 100 Ast,lim/(b d), with Ast,lim found from Mu,lim. State that IS 456 design practice keeps sections under-reinforced. Mention ductility and warning before brittle failure. Some syllabi call these tension-controlled, balanced and compression-controlled sections.

figure.aria: Flowchart from strain compatibility to neutral axis depth, then three branches for under-reinforced, balanced and over-reinforced sections.

chapters.example: A rectangular beam has b = 300 mm, d = 500 mm, fck = 30 N/mm², fy = 500 N/mm² and Ast = 2500 mm². Compute pt,lim and classify the section.
chapters.trap: Calling a section under-reinforced because Ast is small without comparing xu with xu,max; or using the Fe415 limit for Fe500 steel.
chapters.leave: Design of shear reinforcement goes to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: When singly reinforced capacity is insufficient or depth is restricted, compression steel plus extra tension steel add a couple that raises moment capacity.
chapters.depth: Explain when Mu exceeds Mu,lim or depth is restricted. Keep xu = xu,max and add compression steel Asc at effective cover d′. Compression force is 0.36 fck b xu + fsc Asc; tension force is 0.87 fy Ast. Design moment is Mu = Mu,lim + Asc fsc (d − d′), with extra tension steel Ast2 = Asc fsc/(0.87 fy). Obtain fsc from strain compatibility; take fsc = 0.87 fy only when compression steel has yielded. State limits on Asc and Ast. Some syllabi call this compression reinforcement.

figure.aria: Flowchart from excess moment to fixing the neutral axis, sizing compression steel, then adding the matching tension steel.

chapters.example: Design compression and tension steel for b = 250 mm, d = 500 mm, d′ = 50 mm, fck = 25 N/mm², fy = 415 N/mm², Mu = 250 kN·m. Mu,lim is 215.6 kN·m.
chapters.trap: Adding Asc without adding the matching extra tension steel Ast2; or taking fsc = 0.87fy when d′ is large and compression steel has not yielded.
chapters.leave: Bar curtailment and detailing go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A slab cast monolithically with a beam forms a T or L section; the flange in compression adds capacity, but only over an effective width.
chapters.depth: Cover T and L beams cast with a slab. Define effective flange width bf from IS 456 using bw, slab thickness Df, clear span and spacing; do not use the full slab width. If xu ≤ Df, analyse as a rectangular beam of width bf. If xu > Df, use a T-section stress block: concrete force in flange overhangs plus web. Design tension steel and check xu. Mention isolated T-beams and continuous T-beams; some syllabi call these flanged beams.

figure.aria: Flowchart from T-beam dimensions to effective flange width, then a neutral-axis check that chooses rectangular or T-section stress block.

chapters.example: A T-beam has bf = 1000 mm, bw = 300 mm, Df = 100 mm, d = 500 mm, fck = 25 N/mm², fy = 415 N/mm² and Mu = 250 kN·m. Check whether xu lies within the flange and find Ast.
chapters.trap: Using web width bw when the neutral axis is in the flange; or taking the whole slab width as bf.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1; Unit 4 slab behaviour for flange action.
chapters.leave: Shear in flanged beams goes to Unit 3; slab design goes to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Design aid tables and charts for flexure let a designer read steel percentage or moment capacity directly instead of solving the quadratic each time.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Show how standard design aid tables and charts for flexure replace the quadratic solution: enter with Mu/bd², fck and fy, read pt or Ast, and check limits. Cover interpolation, units and the fact that aids assume the standard stress block and under-reinforced sections. Keep derivation out. Some syllabi call this use of design aids for flexure.

figure.title: Design aid lookup
figure.aria: A small lookup table: beam dimensions and moment lead to a read steel percentage and the corresponding steel area.

chapters.example: For b = 230 mm, d = 400 mm, fck = 25 N/mm², fy = 415 N/mm² and Mu = 120 kN·m, a design aid gives pt = 1.35%. Find Ast and choose 20 mm bars.
chapters.trap: Reading pt as a fraction instead of a percentage, or using a chart for the wrong fck/fy.
chapters.leave: Derivation of the tables goes to a handbook; this chapter teaches only reading and checking.

chapters.idea: A beam must also remain usable: deflection and crack width are checked at service loads, not only at collapse.
chapters.depth: Cover IS 456 serviceability: deflection limits total span/250 and after partitions span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is less; simplified span/depth check with modification factors for tension steel, compression steel and flanged sections; crack control by bar spacing, cover and distribution steel. State that service loads and not factored loads are used. Mention short-term and long-term deflection; creep and shrinkage. Some syllabi call this deflection control and crack control.

figure.aria: Flowchart of serviceability checks: service loads, deflection, crack control, then either detailing or revision.

chapters.example: A simply supported beam has span 6.0 m and computed total deflection 22 mm. The partition is installed after construction and computed deflection after partition is 19 mm. Check the IS 456 deflection limits.
chapters.trap: Using factored loads for deflection, or comparing after-partition deflection with span/250 instead of span/350.
chapters.leave: Detailed crack-width formula and shear cracks go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Before concrete cracks, a beam behaves elastically; transforming steel into equivalent concrete lets you compute stresses and the cracking moment Mcr.
chapters.depth: Define modular ratio m = Es/Ec with Es = 200,000 N/mm² and Ec = 5000√fck N/mm². For an uncracked transformed section, replace tension steel by (m − 1)Ast because concrete is displaced; find the neutral axis by first moment of areas and I about it. Cracking moment Mcr = fr I / yt, where fr = 0.7√fck N/mm² is flexural tensile strength and yt is distance from neutral axis to extreme tension fibre. Distinguish uncracked gross section from cracked transformed section used for steel stress after cracking.

figure.aria: Flowchart from an uncracked section through modular ratio and transformed steel to the cracking moment formula.

chapters.example: For b = 300 mm, D = 500 mm, d = 450 mm, Ast = 1200 mm² and fck = 25 N/mm², find m and the uncracked transformed-section cracking moment Mcr. Use Es = 200,000 N/mm² and Ec = 5000√fck.
chapters.trap: Using mAst instead of (m − 1)Ast for tension steel in an uncracked transformed section, or using the cracked section I to compute Mcr.
chapters.leave: Working stress design of cracked sections goes to Unit 1; prestress losses go to Unit 6.
